name: Animal Welfare Atlas
description: A curated map of evidence about the lives and experiences of sentient animals, plus a separately labeled collection of ideas about possible futures.

entries.name: Our World in Data
entries.summary: A broad, chart-led synthesis of global agriculture, food systems, biodiversity, and animal welfare. Its animal-focused work connects production statistics with questions about confinement, slaughter, and the number of animals affected.
entries.usefulness: The best starting point for putting animal welfare into a global quantitative context, with transparent charts that usually expose their underlying data.
entries.caveat: Many datasets measure production or animal counts rather than lived experience. Data licenses and definitions vary by underlying source.
entries.access: HTML, CSV and JSON chart data
entries.reuse: OWID-authored material is generally CC BY 4.0; underlying datasets can have separate terms.

entries.name: Food and Agriculture Organization
entries.summary: The primary international source for country-reported livestock, slaughter, fisheries, and aquaculture statistics. FAOSTAT and FishStat provide long-run, cross-country records used by many later estimates.
entries.usefulness: Essential for tracing claims about how many animals are raised, slaughtered, caught, or farmed back to official reporting systems.
entries.caveat: These are production statistics, not a welfare census. Countries differ in coverage and reporting quality, and fish are often recorded by weight rather than individual count.
entries.access: Data portals, bulk downloads and APIs
entries.reuse: FAO provides explicit data terms; check the terms attached to each product.

entries.name: Faunalytics
entries.summary: A large research library and original-research program covering farmed animals, wildlife, companion animals, animal use, public attitudes, and advocacy outcomes. Entries translate academic studies into searchable summaries.
entries.usefulness: An unusually efficient discovery layer for finding evidence spread across disciplines and for seeing what is known, uncertain, or understudied.
entries.caveat: It is an animal-advocacy research organization, so topic selection reflects that mission. Summaries are a guide to—not a substitute for—the underlying studies.
entries.access: Browser HTML and reports; automated requests may be blocked
entries.reuse: Publicly readable; review its terms before reproducing or redistributing material.

entries.name: Animal Clock
entries.summary: A real-time visual counter that turns annual estimates of animals killed for food in the United States into rates that are easier to comprehend. It includes terrestrial animals and estimated wild-caught and farmed aquatic animals.
entries.usefulness: Useful as an intuition-building illustration of scale and of how dramatically totals change when aquatic animals are counted as individuals.
entries.caveat: This is a U.S.-focused visualization, not a live census. Source years and estimation methods differ by category and should be checked before quoting a number.
entries.access: Interactive web page with source notes
entries.reuse: No clear site-wide open license identified; link and cite rather than reproduce.

entries.name: PubMed Central
entries.summary: The U.S. National Library of Medicine’s full-text archive of biomedical and life-science research. It contains open-access reviews and studies on pain, cognition, affective states, welfare indicators, and animal consciousness across many taxa.
entries.usefulness: A primary route to the scientific literature itself, including article text, references, figures, and machine-readable records rather than only secondary summaries.
entries.caveat: Coverage is biomedical rather than welfare-specific, and inclusion in the archive does not settle a scientific claim. Search quality and study appraisal still matter.
entries.access: HTML, XML, APIs and bulk services
entries.reuse: Article-level licenses vary; PMC access does not make every article unrestricted.

references.label: Searching for Animal Sentience: a systematic review

entries.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
entries.summary: A scholar-maintained reference work with careful entries on animal consciousness, animal moral status, pain, ethics, and the philosophy of mind. Articles map arguments, terminology, and disagreements to extensive bibliographies.
entries.usefulness: Provides neutral conceptual scaffolding for understanding why sentience matters morally and where empirical questions end and ethical premises begin.
entries.caveat: It is a philosophy reference, not a source of global animal counts or direct welfare measurements. Entries synthesize debates rather than deliver a single verdict.
entries.reuse: Free to read but copyrighted; follow Stanford’s terms for reuse.

entries.name: Animal Sentience
entries.summary: An open repository that hosts the journal Animal Sentience alongside a broader collection of human–animal studies. The journal pairs target articles with many expert commentaries and author responses.
entries.usefulness: Especially valuable for seeing scientific and philosophical claims tested from multiple disciplinary perspectives rather than presented without challenge.
entries.caveat: The repository spans many subjects and viewpoints. Commentary can clarify a debate but is not equivalent to independent replication or systematic review.
entries.access: Repository records, PDFs and article metadata
entries.reuse: Licensing is attached at the item or journal level; verify before reuse.

entries.name: Welfare Footprint Project
entries.summary: A quantitative framework for comparing animal-welfare problems through the intensity and duration of negative experiences, together with the number of animals affected. Applied studies estimate cumulative time spent in pain under different production scenarios.
entries.usefulness: Moves beyond counting animals or deaths by asking how bad experiences are and how long they last—the dimensions needed for meaningful welfare comparison.
entries.caveat: Pain categories and duration estimates require judgment under uncertainty. Results are scenario-specific and should not be treated as universal constants.
entries.evidence_type: Quantitative welfare framework and applied studies
entries.access: HTML methods, reports and downloadable outputs
entries.reuse: Many project outputs state open licenses; verify the license on each item.

entries.name: Fishcount
entries.summary: A specialist effort to estimate the number of individual fish caught from the wild and produced in aquaculture, translating tonnage statistics into animal counts and documenting common capture and slaughter practices.
entries.usefulness: Corrects a major unit-of-measure blind spot: fisheries are usually reported in tonnes, while welfare attaches to individual animals and their experiences.
entries.caveat: Individual counts are modeled ranges, not direct observations. They depend on species composition, average weights, FAO records, and assumptions that carry substantial uncertainty.
entries.evidence_type: Modeled count estimates and literature synthesis
entries.access: Plain HTML, reports and calculation notes
entries.reuse: No clear site-wide open license identified; cite estimates and methods carefully.

entries.name: Sea Around Us
entries.summary: A research initiative that reconstructs marine catches by country, taxon, fishing sector, and destination, including components often missing from official landings such as discards and unreported catch.
entries.usefulness: Provides a fuller empirical picture of human impacts on wild aquatic animals and the scale hidden when only reported commercial landings are counted.
entries.caveat: Catch is a pressure and scale proxy, not a direct measure of suffering or welfare. Reconstructed values are estimates and uncertainty differs across places and periods.
entries.reuse: Data are available for research use with attribution; consult current terms and citation guidance.

entries.name: Wild Animal Initiative
entries.summary: A research organization focused on the welfare of free-living animals. Its work develops field methods, reviews welfare-relevant ecology, maps research priorities, and supports an emerging academic discipline.
entries.usefulness: One of the clearest gateways from ecological facts—disease, injury, hunger, weather, reproduction, predation—to questions about animals’ actual quality of life.
entries.caveat: The field is young and direct population-level welfare measurements remain scarce. The organization is mission-driven, and many outputs identify questions rather than settle them.
entries.evidence_type: Research program, reviews and field methods
entries.reuse: Publicly readable; no verified site-wide open license.

entries.name: Wild Animal Welfare Committee
entries.summary: An independent UK committee examining the welfare of free-living wild animals affected by human activities. It publishes evidence-led perspectives on management, policy, and how welfare should be assessed in wildlife decisions.
entries.usefulness: A practical bridge between welfare science and real decisions about wild animals, including cases where conservation, population control, and individual welfare can point in different directions.
entries.caveat: Its scope is primarily UK policy and human interventions, not a global estimate of welfare in nature.
entries.evidence_type: Independent expert analysis and policy advice
entries.reuse: Check the terms attached to individual committee publications.

entries.name: EU Animals in Science / ALURES
entries.summary: The European Commission’s transparency system for animals used in scientific procedures. ALURES reports animals, uses, purposes, species, origins, genetic status, and the actual severity assigned to procedures across EU member states and Norway.
entries.usefulness: One of the few multi-country official systems that reports experienced severity as well as counts, and that provides bulk exports alongside non-technical project summaries.
entries.caveat: This is regional, not global. Definitions, participating countries, and data-mining comparability change across years, and official severity classes remain coarse.
entries.evidence_type: Official regional statistics and project records
entries.access: HTML dashboards and full dataset exports
entries.reuse: European Commission reuse rules apply; inspect dataset-specific notices.

entries.name: The Hedonistic Imperative
entries.summary: David Pearce’s long-running archive arguing that biotechnology could replace suffering with gradients of well-being across all sentient life. It connects genetics, consciousness, superintelligence, animal ethics, and the redesign of ecosystems.
entries.usefulness: The most developed single-author vision of a post-Darwinian future in which preventing suffering extends beyond humans and domesticated animals.
entries.caveat: A philosophical and technological program, not an empirical forecast. Its feasibility, assumptions about consciousness, and prescriptions are strongly contested.
entries.reuse: No clear site-wide open license identified; link and quote only within ordinary citation norms.

entries.name: Herbivorize Predators
entries.summary: A focused case for using directed evolution to transform rather than eliminate predatory species, aiming for ecosystems in which sentient animals no longer need to kill other animals to survive.
entries.usefulness: Makes one radical response to wild-animal suffering concrete enough to inspect, compare with alternatives, and challenge on ecological and ethical grounds.
entries.caveat: Highly conjectural and prescriptive. Ecological safety, technical feasibility, governance, animal interests, and unintended effects are unresolved.
entries.reuse: Publicly crawlable; verify rights before reproducing text or graphics.

entries.name: Sentience Institute
entries.summary: A research organization studying moral-circle expansion: how societies come to include previously excluded sentient beings. Its work spans animals, social movements, technological change, and the possible moral status of digital minds.
entries.usefulness: Connects concern for animals today with the institutions and historical processes that may determine which beings future societies—and future AI systems—take seriously.
entries.caveat: Research is shaped by effective-altruist and long-term-future concerns. Historical analogies and forecasts about digital minds remain uncertain.
entries.access: HTML reports, articles, podcasts and datasets
entries.reuse: Check the license or terms for each publication and dataset.

references.label: Moral circle expansion and extinction risk

entries.name: Center for Reducing Suffering
entries.summary: A research center developing suffering-focused ethics and work on preventing futures with suffering on an enormous scale. Topics include wild animals, moral status, artificial minds, AI governance, and institutions.
entries.usefulness: Surfaces worst-case possibilities that standard animal-welfare and AI-governance discussions often omit, while giving their ethical premises explicit treatment.
entries.caveat: Explicitly normative and focused on severe suffering. Conclusions can depend on contested population ethics, low-probability scenarios, and uncertain models of the far future.
entries.reuse: Publicly readable; check publication-level terms before reuse.

entries.name: Essays on Reducing Suffering
entries.summary: Brian Tomasik’s extensive essay archive on wild-animal suffering, insect sentience, population ethics, artificial minds, simulations, and far-future outcomes. It includes exploratory calculations as well as philosophical arguments.
entries.usefulness: A wide-ranging record of neglected questions and unusual implications, especially where animal welfare intersects with computation and long-run technological change.
entries.caveat: A personal and intentionally exploratory archive. Many estimates are rough, views have evolved over time, and speculative pieces should not be mistaken for consensus research.
entries.evidence_type: Personal philosophical and quantitative essay archive
entries.reuse: No verified site-wide open license; cite individual essays and dates.

entries.name: Qualia Research Institute
entries.summary: A research organization exploring formal theories of consciousness and valence—the positive or negative character of experience—and how future technology might measure or alter them.
entries.usefulness: Relevant to the long-run question behind welfare measurement: whether the quality of experience can be understood precisely enough to compare or engineer, including in unfamiliar minds.
entries.caveat: Frontier, highly speculative work with limited direct animal-welfare application today. Its theories of consciousness and valence are not scientific consensus.
entries.access: HTML essays, papers and open-source code
entries.reuse: Licensing varies across writing, papers and code; inspect each item.
